summary: Defines the Reason header field for SIP. It lets a request or response say why it was sent, such as carrying a cause value from another protocol, for example when a call is cancelled or when a message is created because of an earlier one. It was later updated by RFCs 8606 and 9366.

plainLanguage.summary: When someone hangs up, it helps to know why. The Reason header is a little note attached to a phone message that explains the cause.

questions: what is the sip reason header
how does sip report why a call was cancelled
what is the q.850 cause in sip
subtitle: A SIP header field that says why a request was sent, carrying a SIP status code or a Q.850 cause value.

tldr.problem: The same SIP request, such as CANCEL, can be sent for very different reasons, and the receiver cannot tell them apart. A call picked up elsewhere should not be logged as a missed call, for example.
tldr.mechanism: The Reason header field carries a protocol name (SIP or Q.850), a numeric cause and optional free text, so a request can say what triggered it.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that implementations are free to ignore, and it has been updated by RFC 8606 and RFC 9366. It was also meant to carry a final error code inside a provisional response to help with the HERFP problem.

today: RFC 3326 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8606 and RFC 9366, so read it together with those documents. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Request Needs a Reason
sections.content:
A SIP request can be issued for several different reasons. A CANCEL may be sent because the call completed on another branch, or because the caller gave up before anyone answered. The protocol behavior is the same in both cases, because alerting stops, but the user interface may differ: the second case can be logged as a missed call, while the first should not be.

Third party call controllers sometimes send a request after they receive a response from another dialog, and gateways send SIP requests after receiving messages from a different protocol. In both cases the receiving client may want to know what triggered the request. SIP responses already explain why a request failed; this document adds something roughly similar for requests.

The header field was also meant for the Heterogeneous Error Response Forking Problem (HERFP). When an INVITE forks and a branch rejects it because some aspect of the request was unacceptable, the error may never reach the client unless all other branches also reject. The RFC foresees encapsulating the final error response in a provisional response, and names Reason as a candidate for that encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two phone calls can end the same way for different reasons. This note lets the phone tell you which reason it was, so it can treat each one properly.

sections.title: The Reason Header Field
sections.content:
A Reason header field holds one or more values, separated by commas. Each value starts with a protocol and is followed by semicolon-separated parameters: a numeric cause, a quoted text, or any other generic parameter.

Two protocol values are defined. SIP means the cause parameter holds a SIP status code. Q.850 means it holds an ITU-T Q.850 cause value in decimal form. The grammar also allows any other token as a protocol name.

The header field MAY appear in any request within a dialog, in any CANCEL request, and in any response whose status code explicitly allows it. The RFC notes it is usually not needed in responses, because the status code and reason phrase already say enough. It looks most useful for BYE and CANCEL.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has three parts: which rulebook the code comes from, the code number itself, and a few words of plain text for people to read.

sections.title: Rules for Using It
sections.content:
Any SIP status code MAY appear in the Reason header field of a request. The RFC distinguishes two kinds. Codes that describe the user or the session parameters, such as 486 (Busy Here) or 488 (Not Acceptable Here), are typically useful for implementing services. Codes that report errors about a request, such as 405 (Method not allowed), are typically useful for debugging.

A message MAY contain more than one Reason value, but each one MUST use a different protocol value, for example one SIP and one Q.850. An implementation is free to ignore Reason values it does not understand.

A proxy that generates a CANCEL after receiving a CANCEL from the previous hop that contains a Reason header field SHOULD copy it into the new request.

Clients and servers are free to ignore this header field. It has no impact on protocol processing.
sections.plainLanguage: You can attach one note per rulebook, and a phone that does not understand a note can just skip it. A middleman who passes along a hang-up should pass the note along too.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four scenarios. In call completed elsewhere, a forking proxy gets a 200 (OK) from one branch and puts that status code in the Reason header of the CANCEL it sends to the other branches.

In refusing an offer that comes in a response, a client sends an empty INVITE and gets an unacceptable offer in a 200. It sends an ACK with a correctly formatted answer, then immediately sends a BYE carrying 488 in a Reason header.

In third party call control, a controller tries to connect users A and B, but B is busy, so the controller sends A a BYE with 486 (Busy Here).

In ISUP interworking, a PSTN gateway has sent an INVITE and then receives a REL (release) message from the ISUP side. It sends a CANCEL carrying the Q.850 cause value 16 (Normal Call Clearing) from that message.
sections.plainLanguage: If one friend answers a group call, the phone company tells everyone else "someone picked up already", so nobody thinks they missed a call.

sections.title: Registration
sections.content:
The document registers the new SIP header field Reason under Section 27 of RFC 3261. It also asks IANA to create a sub-registry called Reason Protocols, which pairs each protocol value with what its cause field means.

A registered reason protocol MUST refer to an ITU-T Recommendation number, an IETF protocol name, or the recognized protocol identifier from another standardization organization. At the time of writing, the only entries are SIP (a status code, defined in RFC 3261) and Q.850 (a cause value in decimal representation, defined in ITU-T Q.850).
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of which rulebooks may be named in the note. It started with just two entries.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The only risk the RFC names is in a HERFP scenario. If an attacker spoofs the Reason header field in a response, or removes it, the client may be unable to update its previous request properly. That would make session establishment impossible.

For this reason the RFC says the header field is RECOMMENDED to be protected by a suitable integrity mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad guy changes or removes the note, your phone may not know how to fix its call, so the note should be sealed so nobody can tamper with it.

data.title: Reason header syntax
data.code:
Reason            =  "Reason" HCOLON reason-value *(COMMA reason-value)
reason-value      =  protocol *(SEMI reason-params)
protocol          =  "SIP" / "Q.850" / token
reason-params     =  protocol-cause / reason-text
                     / reason-extension
protocol-cause    =  "cause" EQUAL cause
cause             =  1*DIGIT
reason-text       =  "text" EQUAL quoted-string
reason-extension  =  generic-param

Reason: SIP ;cause=200 ;text="Call completed elsewhere"
Reason: Q.850 ;cause=16 ;text="Terminated"
Reason: SIP ;cause=600 ;text="Busy Everywhere"
Reason: SIP ;cause=580 ;text="Precondition Failure"

messages.label: CANCEL (Q.850 16)
messages.note: Carries the Q.850 cause value of the REL.
